title: A 1,800 km cloud on Mars freezes out of thin air with no dust to start it, a model says
body: On 7 October 2026 a team at the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique, Paris, reported in [Nature Geoscience](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41561-026-02089-9) that the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud on Mars is best explained by ice forming straight out of water vapour, with no particle to start it, never seen before in a planet’s atmosphere. Clouds on Earth begin on seeds: every droplet or ice crystal condenses on a speck of dust, salt or soot, so the air need hold only a little more water than it can keep. The ribbon over the Martian volcano, up to about 1,800 km long at about 45 km altitude, could not be reproduced that way. In the model, as [Astronomy magazine reports](https://www.astronomy.com/science/the-weird-science-behind-mars-weirdest-cloud/), wind lifts moist air up the western flank in minutes, cooling it about 30 °C in 10 minutes to below −143 °C, until it holds about 100,000 times the water it can keep; with only about 0.1 dust grain per cubic centimetre that high, the vapour freezes on its own, and winds stretch the crystals west at about 610 km/h for about three hours. The model still misses the cloud’s exact timing and length.

slides.question: The cloud that grows from the Martian volcano Arsia Mons each spring morning stretches up to how many kilometres?
slides.explanation: Up to about 1,800 km, under 200 km wide, at about 45 km altitude. Its tail stretches west at about 610 km/h, so the full length takes about three hours.

slides.alt: Animation on a rust Martian sky: a pale ribbon of ice cloud streaming west from the volcano Arsia Mons, vapour gathering on a dust speck, a parcel of air climbing the slope as a thermometer falls to −143 °C and a bar reaches 100,000× saturation, ice crystals, and the 1,800 km tail.

slides.prompt: Make ice form in a box of air that has no dust seeds at all. How far past saturation do you have to push the vapour?
slides.takeaway: With seeds, ice forms barely over saturation; with none, only at about 100,000 times, the Mars model’s figure. Earth’s air is never that clean or that supersaturated, which is why this had never been seen.

slides.heading: Two ways to make ice in the air

left.label: With a seed
left.text: Water vapour settles on a speck of dust, salt or soot. Earth’s air always has specks, so clouds form barely over saturation.

right.label: Without a seed
right.text: Vapour must be pushed far beyond saturation, about 100,000 times in the Mars model, before it freezes on its own. Never seen in nature before.

slides.heading: A morning at Arsia Mons, in the model

steps.label: Sunrise: wind climbs the western slope
Moist air rises km in minutes, cools 30 °C
Vapour freezes without dust, 200 per cm³
Winds stretch the tail west at 610 km/h
After ~3 hours it lets go and evaporates

slides.question: Why could water vapour freeze without any dust in the Mars model of the Arsia Mons cloud?
options: Mars has too little gravity to stop it
The air was warmer than on Earth
slides.explanation: Air lifted up the volcano cooled about 30 °C in 10 minutes to below −143 °C, far too fast and far too clean, with about 0.1 dust grain per cm³, for seeds, so the vapour froze on its own.
